traditions/hutterite/summary: Anabaptists who practise community of goods, originating in Moravia in 1528 and named after Jakob Hutter, their leader until his execution in 1536. They flourished in Moravia, then endured persecution and migration through Slovakia, Transylvania and Ukraine before resettling in the Dakotas in the 1870s. Most now live in agricultural colonies in the Canadian prairies and the northern United States.
traditions/hutterite/distinctives/0: Community of goods based on Acts 2 and 4
traditions/hutterite/distinctives/1: Living in colonies (Bruderhöfe) of roughly 60–150 people
traditions/hutterite/distinctives/3: Hutterisch dialect and historic sermons read in worship
traditions/hutterite/profile/authority: Scripture and the sixteenth-century writings of Peter Riedemann (Rechenschaft, 1540s) and early Hutterite sermons.
traditions/hutterite/profile/salvation: Surrender of self and property to God and the community (Gelassenheit) as the path of discipleship.
traditions/hutterite/profile/sacraments: Adult baptism and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/hutterite/profile/eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return and judgment.
traditions/hutterite/profile/governance: Colony led by a minister and elected council; three main branches (Schmiedeleut, Dariusleut, Lehrerleut).
traditions/hutterite/profile/worship: Daily evening services and Sunday worship with readings of historic sermons.
traditions/hutterite/status: Active; c. 50,000 people in about 500 colonies.
traditions/quaker/summary: A movement begun in England in the 1650s under George Fox, who taught that Christ 'the inward light' can speak directly to every person without clergy, sacraments or set liturgy. Severely persecuted in Restoration England, Quakers founded Pennsylvania under William Penn (1681) and became pioneers of abolition, prison reform and peacemaking. Today Friends range from unprogrammed silent meetings to evangelical pastoral churches, with the largest numbers in Kenya.
traditions/quaker/distinctives/0: The Inward Light of Christ in every person
traditions/quaker/distinctives/1: Meeting for worship in expectant silence (unprogrammed tradition)
traditions/quaker/distinctives/2: No outward sacraments or ordained clergy
traditions/quaker/distinctives/3: Testimonies of peace, simplicity, integrity and equality
traditions/quaker/distinctives/4: Early equality of women in ministry
traditions/quaker/profile/authority: The living guidance of the Spirit of Christ, tested against Scripture and the discernment of the meeting.
traditions/quaker/profile/salvation: Inward transformation by the Light of Christ; early Friends taught the possibility of perfection (freedom from sin).
traditions/quaker/profile/sacraments: No outward sacraments; baptism and communion are understood as inward, spiritual realities.
traditions/quaker/profile/eschatology: Early Friends proclaimed that 'Christ has come to teach his people himself', a realised emphasis on the present kingdom.
traditions/quaker/profile/governance: Business meetings seeking unity under divine guidance, organised in monthly and yearly meetings without clergy (pastoral meetings have pastors).
traditions/quaker/profile/worship: Unprogrammed silent worship where anyone may minister; programmed meetings with hymns and sermons in evangelical yearly meetings.
traditions/quaker/profile/canon: The Protestant canon, held as secondary to the Spirit who gave it.
traditions/quaker/status: Active; c. 377,000 Friends worldwide (2017), about half in Africa.
traditions/baptist/summary: Churches that arose among English Separatists in exile in Amsterdam, where John Smyth and Thomas Helwys baptised believers in 1609, influenced by contact with Mennonites. General (Arminian) and Particular (Calvinist) Baptist streams developed in England, and Baptists became the largest Protestant family in the United States, including major African American denominations. Strong advocates of religious liberty, Baptists launched the modern missionary movement through William Carey (1792) and are now numerous in Nigeria, Brazil, India's north-east and Myanmar.
traditions/baptist/distinctives/2: Soul liberty and separation of church and state
traditions/baptist/distinctives/4: Strong commitment to evangelism and mission
traditions/baptist/profile/authority: Scripture as the sole and sufficient authority; confessions (e.g. the Second London Confession 1689, Baptist Faith and Message) are voluntary statements, not creeds.
traditions/baptist/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ, with a conscious conversion experience; Calvinist and Arminian views both present.
traditions/baptist/profile/sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper, usually understood as memorial and testimony.
traditions/baptist/profile/eschatology: Diverse: premillennial (often dispensational) views are common in North America; others amillennial or postmillennial.
traditions/baptist/profile/governance: Congregational, with pastors and deacons; voluntary associations and conventions.
traditions/baptist/profile/worship: Free-church worship centred on preaching, hymns and gospel music, with altar calls in many traditions.
traditions/baptist/status: Active; c. 47 million baptised believers in BWA churches (2019), and more outside it (e.g. the Southern Baptist Convention).
traditions/unitarian/summary: A tradition affirming the unity of God rather than the Trinity, and so outside historic Nicene orthodoxy. Antitrinitarian churches appeared in the Reformation era in Poland (the Polish Brethren, influenced by Faustus Socinus) and Transylvania, where the Edict of Torda (1568) tolerated the church of Francis Dávid. In New England, liberal Congregationalists led by William Ellery Channing formed the American Unitarian Association (1825). Merging with the Universalists in 1961, the Unitarian Universalist Association became a pluralist, largely post-Christian body, while the Hungarian Unitarian Church remains explicitly Christian.
traditions/unitarian/distinctives/0: God is one person; Jesus is a uniquely inspired human teacher and exemplar
traditions/unitarian/distinctives/1: Reason and conscience in interpreting religion
traditions/unitarian/distinctives/3: Emphasis on ethics, social reform and freedom of belief
traditions/unitarian/distinctives/4: Unitarian Universalism welcomes non-Christian and humanist members
traditions/unitarian/profile/authority: Reason, conscience and experience; Scripture valued as a historical and inspirational source rather than final authority.
traditions/unitarian/profile/salvation: Character and moral growth rather than atonement; Universalist heritage holds that all will ultimately be reconciled to God.
traditions/unitarian/profile/sacraments: No sacraments in the traditional sense; child dedications and communion services in some Christian Unitarian congregations.
traditions/unitarian/profile/eschatology: Little emphasis on final judgment; historically hope for universal salvation and human progress.
traditions/unitarian/profile/worship: Services of readings, hymns, sermons and reflection, varying from liberal Christian to humanist.
traditions/unitarian/profile/canon: No closed canon; the Bible is read alongside other sources of wisdom.
traditions/unitarian/status: Active but small: c. 150,000 in the Unitarian Universalist Association (US), plus Unitarian churches in Transylvania and Britain; outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
traditions/general-baptists/summary: The earliest English Baptists, descended from the congregation of John Smyth and Thomas Helwys (Amsterdam 1609, London 1612). They were called 'General' because they held that Christ died for all people generally (an Arminian view of the atonement). Many older General Baptist congregations drifted toward Unitarianism in the eighteenth century; the evangelical New Connexion (1770) merged with the Particular Baptists in 1891, and American heirs include the Free Will Baptists and the General Association of General Baptists.
traditions/general-baptists/distinctives: Early advocacy of liberty of conscience (Helwys, 1612)
Messengers linking congregations into an Assembly
Some practised laying on of hands after baptism (Hebrews 6:1-2)
traditions/general-baptists/profile/auth: Scripture alone, interpreted within the gathered congregation; confessions such as the Standard Confession (1660) as summaries, not binding creeds.
traditions/general-baptists/profile/salv: Christ died for all; grace enables a free response of faith, and believers can fall away.
traditions/general-baptists/profile/sacr: Two ordinances, baptism of professing believers and the Lord's Supper; originally baptism by pouring, later immersion.
traditions/general-baptists/profile/esch: Expectation of Christ's return, resurrection and final judgment.
traditions/general-baptists/profile/gove: Congregational, with messengers and a General Assembly linking churches.
traditions/general-baptists/profile/wors: Plain preaching services; some early congregations resisted congregational hymn singing.
traditions/general-baptists/status: Historic as a separate English movement; continues in small General Baptist bodies and in the Free Will Baptist tradition.
traditions/particular-baptists/summary: Calvinistic Baptists who emerged from London Independent (Congregationalist) churches in the 1630s. They held that Christ died for a 'particular' people, the elect. Their First (1644) and Second (1677, published 1689) London Confessions closely follow Reformed theology; leaders included William Kiffin, Hanserd Knollys, Benjamin Keach and later John Gill and Andrew Fuller, whose evangelical Calvinism inspired the Baptist Missionary Society (1792).
traditions/particular-baptists/distincti: Calvinist soteriology with believers' baptism by immersion
Covenant theology in a Baptist key
Fuller's 'evangelical Calvinism' launched modern Protestant missions
traditions/particular-baptists/profile/a: Scripture alone; the Second London Confession (1689) as a widely used standard among Reformed Baptists.
traditions/particular-baptists/profile/s: Unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual grace and perseverance of the saints.
Baptism by immersion of professing believers and the Lord's Supper as ordinances, often with a spiritual-presence view.
traditions/particular-baptists/profile/e: Generally amillennial or postmillennial in the classical period; premillennialism later spread among some.
traditions/particular-baptists/profile/g: Congregational, with associations for fellowship and mission.
traditions/particular-baptists/profile/w: Preaching-centred services; Benjamin Keach championed congregational hymn singing.
traditions/particular-baptists/status: Historic name; the tradition continues in Reformed Baptist churches and as a strand within most Baptist bodies.
traditions/southern-baptist-convention/s: Founded at Augusta, Georgia, in 1845 when Baptists of the slave states separated from the national Baptist mission societies over the appointment of slaveholders as missionaries. The SBC grew into the largest Protestant denomination in the United States, with a powerful cooperative mission programme (Cooperative Program, 1925; International Mission Board). A 'conservative resurgence' from 1979 shifted its seminaries and agencies toward biblical inerrancy. In 1995 it formally apologised for its origins in the defence of slavery and for its support of segregation.
traditions/southern-baptist-convention/d: Cooperative Program funding of missions and seminaries
Strong emphasis on evangelism and church planting
Complementarian limits on women as pastors (2000; affirmed 2023)
Autonomy of local churches within voluntary convention structures
traditions/southern-baptist-convention/p: Scripture as inspired and without error; the Baptist Faith and Message (1925, 1963, 2000) as a consensus statement, not a creed binding churches.
Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ; once saved, always saved (perseverance) is widely held; Calvinist and non-Calvinist streams coexist.
Two ordinances: believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Return of Christ, judgment, heaven and hell; premillennialism common but no single view required.

Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. The annual convention elects officers and trustees of agencies.
Revivalist-style services with preaching, congregational song and an invitation to respond.
traditions/southern-baptist-convention/s: Active; c. 12.7 million members in c. 47,000 churches (2024), with membership declining since 2006.
traditions/national-baptist-convention-u: The largest African American denomination, formed in Atlanta in 1895 from three Black Baptist conventions. It sustained missions in Africa and the Caribbean, publishing and schools. Its 1915 split produced the National Baptist Convention of America, and in 1961 supporters of a more activist civil-rights strategy, including Martin Luther King Jr., formed the Progressive National Baptist Convention.
Black-led Baptist institutions independent of white control
Preaching tradition central to Black church life
Missions to Liberia and southern Africa
Churches as centres of community and civil-rights organising
Scripture alone, commonly summarised in the New Hampshire Confession (1833) tradition.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, received in conversion.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
Hope of Christ's return and final deliverance, often linked with themes of exodus and freedom.
Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
Expressive worship with gospel music, call-and-response preaching and devotion services.
Active; one of the largest Black denominations in the United States (membership self-reported in the millions).
